hook.text: The Millau Viaduct's tallest pier is higher than the Eiffel Tower. Cars drive across clouds.

buildup.text: Crossing the Tarn Valley in France required a bridge 1,125 feet above the river.

discovery.text: Seven cable-stayed spans carry the highway 1.5 miles across the valley.

twist.text: The deck was built on one side and pushed out hydraulically — 600 meters at a time.

climax.text: Designed by Norman Foster and Michel Virlogeux — architecture and engineering merged.

punchline.text: Drivers cross a valley so high they pass through the clouds.

quiz.question: How tall is the Millau Viaduct's tallest pier?
options: About half the height of the Statue of Liberty
About the same height as a 10-story building

details.summary: The Millau Viaduct in southern France, designed by engineer Michel Virlogeux and architect Norman Foster, is the world's tallest bridge with one pier reaching 343 meters.
details.whyItMatters: The Millau Viaduct proved that mega-scale bridge engineering and architectural beauty are not mutually exclusive, setting a new standard for infrastructure aesthetics.
takeaways: Its tallest pier at 343 meters makes it the world's tallest bridge structure
The deck was pushed out from both ends using hydraulic launching
Construction took only three years despite the enormous scale

faq.question: How was the Millau Viaduct's deck constructed across such a deep valley?
faq.answer: The steel deck was assembled on the ground at both ends and pushed out over the valley using hydraulic rams on top of temporary pylons placed on each pier. The deck inched forward at about 600 millimeters per cycle, eventually meeting in the middle of the valley.

faq.question: Why was the Millau Viaduct built as a toll road?
faq.answer: The French government used a concession model where the private company Eiffage financed and built the bridge in exchange for collecting tolls for 78 years. This public-private partnership avoided using tax revenue while providing a much-needed bypass for the congested Millau town route.
